---
title: "Six-Sided Die"
subtitle: "Discrete and flat, but perfectly symmetric"
---

```{r}
#| label: simulate
#| code-summary: "Show the simulation code"
source("../R/clt_functions.R")

rgen  <- function(n) sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE)   # n fair rolls
mu    <- 3.5
sigma <- sqrt(35 / 12)       # = 1.708
pop_kurt <- -1.2686          # excess kurtosis of a fair die

coarse <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38, 40, 45, 50,
            60, 75, 100, 200)
exper  <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma)

res    <- exper$results
n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res)
n_std  <- n_by_standard(res)
at     <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ]

save_results(res, "die")
save_summary(res, "Six-sided die", n_main, prediction = "15",
             key_note = "Symmetric: flat shape and discreteness are the only obstacles")
```

::: {.answer-box}
<span class="big">n = `r n_main`</span> under my main standard
(strict standard: ≈ `r n_std[["strict"]]` · lenient standard: `r n_std[["lenient"]]` · my prediction: 15)
:::

## 1. What population am I sampling from?

A fair six-sided die: the values 1 to 6, each with probability 1/6. It is the opposite of a bell curve.
It is **flat** (no peak), **bounded** (no extreme values at all), and **discrete** (only six possible
values). It is, however, perfectly **symmetric**.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean μ | 3.5 |
| Standard deviation σ | √(35/12) ≈ 1.708 |
| Skewness | 0 (symmetric) |
| Excess kurtosis | −1.27 (light tails: flat, no extremes) |
| Theoretical SE of the mean | 1.708/√n |

```{r}
#| label: fig-population
#| fig-cap: "The population: six equally likely values."
#| fig-height: 3.6
style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
barplot(rep(1/6, 6), names.arg = 1:6, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75),
        border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.2), xlab = "Face", ylab = "Probability")
```

## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation?

> **n = 15.** The die is symmetric (skewness 0) but flat and discrete. In my pilot run it clearly failed
> at n = 1 and passed every check at n = 15, so I predicted 15.

## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate?

1. **Coarse grid:** n = `r paste(coarse, collapse = ", ")`. It is denser between 30 and 50 to locate
   the strict standard.
2. **Refinement:** `r if (length(exper$refined)) paste0("every n from ", min(exper$refined), " to ", max(exper$refined)) else "not needed"`.

B = 100,000 sample means per n, seed `r student_id`. For plotting, each histogram bar is one possible
value of the mean. The average of n rolls can only be a multiple of 1/n, so there are 5n + 1 possible values.

## 4. Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-convergence
#| fig-cap: "The four checks. Skewness is zero from the start; the Q-Q correlation is the last check to pass. Orange: theoretical kurtosis −1.27/n."
#| fig-height: 6.5
plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = 0, theory_kurt = pop_kurt)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| fig-cap: "Sampling distribution of the mean of n rolls (one bar per possible value) and the CLT normal curve."
#| fig-height: 6
n_show <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, n_main, 30)
plot_hist_grid(exper, n_show, mu, sigma, step = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q plots. At small n the points form visible steps (discreteness) and an S-shape (light tails)."
#| fig-height: 6
plot_qq_grid(exper, n_show)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-se
#| fig-cap: "Simulated SE (dots) against σ/√n (line)."
#| fig-height: 4.2
plot_se_check(res)
```

The simulated mean stayed within `r f4(max(abs(res$sim_mean - mu)))` of 3.5, and the simulated SE was
within `r pct(max(abs(res$se_ratio - 1)))` of σ/√n at every n.

## 5. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r n_main`}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standards
#| echo: false
standards_table(res)
```

## 6. Why did I choose that value?

- **Skewness never mattered.** It was `r f3(at(1)$skewness)` at n = 1 and stayed near zero, because the
  die is symmetric.
- **The flat shape faded quickly.** Excess kurtosis follows −1.27/n and passed my ±0.5 limit at
  n = `r first_stable_n(res$n, res$kurt_ok)`.
- **The Q-Q correlation was the last check to pass**, at n = `r first_stable_n(res$n, res$qq_ok)`.
  At small n the Q-Q plot is a staircase with an S-shape: the steps come from discreteness, and the S
  comes from the missing tails (a sum of a few dice can never be very far from 3.5).
- At **n = `r n_main`** all four checks pass: skewness `r f3(at(n_main)$skewness)`, kurtosis
  `r f3(at(n_main)$ex_kurtosis)`, Q-Q r `r f4(at(n_main)$qq_cor)`, tails
  `r pct(at(n_main)$lower_tail, 2)` / `r pct(at(n_main)$upper_tail, 2)`. Every larger n also passes.
  `r flip_text(res, n_main)`

## 7. What surprised me?

> I expected the die to stay visibly discrete for a long time, since it only has six values. It passed
> my main standard at n = `r n_main`. What surprised me more is that it also passed the strict standard
> at around n = `r n_std[["strict"]]`. Its skewness was zero from the start, so the only problems were the
> flat shape and the gaps between possible values. With n rolls the mean can take 5n + 1 different values,
> and by n = 40 the gaps are less than a tenth of a standard error. So even for a discrete distribution
> like a die, a larger n improves the approximation quite well.
